subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: An ectopic pregnancy is implantation of a fertilized egg outside the uterine cavity, most often in the fallopian tube. Prompt diagnosis and treatment prevent rupture, hemorrhage, and infertility.

sections.p: Ectopic pregnancy occurs when the embryo implants in a non‑uterine site, typically the ampullary portion of the tube. Diagnosis requires a positive pregnancy test plus evidence that the gestational sac is not intrauterine.
b: Positive β‑hCG with no intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal ultrasound
Serial β‑hCG that rises slower than the expected 66% per 48 h in normal pregnancy

t.b: Is the level above the discriminatory zone (~1500 IU/L) without intrauterine sac? Supports ectopic.

sections.p: The American Society for Reproductive Medicine grades tubal ectopic pregnancy by size, presence of cardiac activity, and rupture risk. Stages guide medical vs surgical management.
b: Stage I: <3 cm, no cardiac activity, stable
Stage II: 3‑5 cm or cardiac activity, stable
Stage III: rupture or hemodynamic instability

sections.p: Risk factors disrupt tubal transport or mucosal integrity, allowing implantation outside the uterus.
b: Prior tubal surgery or pelvic inflammatory disease (most common)
Previous ectopic pregnancy
In vitro fertilisation
Smoking
Tubal pathology from tuberculosis (relevant in low‑resource settings)
Use of intra‑uterine device (copper) – rare but possible

sections.p: Patients often present with early pregnancy symptoms plus pain or bleeding.
b: Unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain
Spotting or light vaginal bleeding
Shoulder tip pain if intraperitoneal bleed
Syncope or tachycardia if rupture

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with targeted tests to confirm location and assess stability.
b: Assess hemodynamic status before imaging

t.b: Low levels (<5 ng/mL) favor non‑viable ectopic; not definitive
Detect intra‑abdominal blood; positive fluid indicates possible rupture.

sections.p: Rapid deterioration signals rupture and massive hemorrhage, a surgical emergency.
b: Sudden worsening pain
Hypotension or tachycardia
Abdominal rigidity
Drop in hemoglobin

sections.p: Treat the ectopic while preserving fertility when possible. Choose medical or surgical therapy based on stability, size, and β‑hCG level.
b: Methotrexate (systemic) for stable patients with β‑hCG <5000 IU/L, no cardiac activity, and mass <3.5 cm – inhibits trophoblastic DNA synthesis
Laparoscopic salpingostomy or salpingectomy for rupture or contraindication to methotrexate – removes ectopic tissue while sparing tube when feasible
Supportive IV fluids and blood transfusion if hemorrhagic

sections.p: Monitor β‑hCG until undetectable to ensure resolution and counsel on future pregnancy risk.
b: Serial β‑hCG weekly until <5 IU/L
Counsel delayed conception (≥3 months) after treatment
Discuss contraception; copper IUD is safe even after prior ectopic

sections.p: Other early‑pregnancy conditions can mimic ectopic signs.
b: Corpus luteum cyst – can appear as adnexal mass but lacks β‑hCG rise
Miscarriage (incomplete) – bleeding and pain but intrauterine sac may be seen
Appendicitis – right lower quadrant pain without pregnancy signs

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Very low β‑hCG early in ectopic may be below discriminatory zone, appearing normal
Ultrasound may miss a small tubal pregnancy if operator inexperienced

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with fainting or dizziness
Rapidly rising heart rate or low blood pressure
Shoulder tip pain indicating intra‑abdominal bleed

faq.q: Can an IUD cause ectopic pregnancy?
faq.a: A copper IUD greatly reduces overall pregnancy risk; if pregnancy occurs, the relative chance of it being ectopic is higher, but the IUD itself is not a direct cause.

faq.q: Why is methotrexate preferred over surgery in some cases?
faq.a: Methotrexate avoids surgery, preserves tubal anatomy, and is effective when the ectopic is small, unruptured, and the patient is hemodynamically stable.

faq.q: What is the role of serial β‑hCG in management?
faq.a: It confirms treatment success; a falling level >15% per 48 h indicates resolution, while plateauing or rising levels suggest treatment failure.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria for ectopic pregnancy and the role of the discriminatory β‑hCG level.
Explain how you would decide between medical and surgical management in a stable patient.
List the red‑flag signs that mandate urgent surgical intervention.
